questions.text: What is the minimum API concentration change that must be detected (e.g., % w/w) to support process control?

What is the maximum allowable latency between powder passing the probe and a usable concentration readout?

concept.summary: Insert a diffuse‑reflection NIR probe into the powder stream of the feed frame; optionally add a contact Raman probe for side‑by‑side comparison. Light is delivered via silica fiber to a bench‑top NIR spectrometer; Raman uses a separate fiber to a [to be agreed with the customer] Raman spectrometer.

risks: Powder dust may foul probe windows; regular cleaning required.
Temperature fluctuations could affect NIR baseline; need temperature compensation.
Raman probe cost and alignment complexity may be higher than NIR.
Calibration transfer from lab to in‑line may require robust chemometric models.

steps: Collect representative powder blend samples covering the expected API range.
Acquire reference API concentrations by an established lab method (e.g., HPLC).
Record NIR diffuse‑reflection spectra with the proposed probe under process‑like conditions.
Build a chemometric calibration (e.g., PLS) and validate on held‑out samples.
Repeat steps with Raman probe for side‑by‑side comparison.
Assess prediction error, response time, and probe robustness in the feed frame.

Validate the model on samples not used to build it (held-out samples, e.g. from other patients, batches or days) before drawing any conclusion; a model built on few samples can fit them without generalising.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If the NIR model meets the agreed‑upon accuracy and latency, it will be selected; otherwise Raman performance will be evaluated as a backup.
